The study was approved by The University of Auckland Human Participants Ethics Committee (reference C. OKN no. 2011066).
The OKN detection method involves three main steps: head tracking, head stabilization, and pupil center and limbus edge tracking.
The method uses consumer-grade video equipment to track head and eye movements.
The sensitivity and specificity of the OKN detection method are 89.13% and 98.54%, respectively.
The method compares well with results obtained from a clinically trained assessor (85%).
The OKN detection results are based on the analysis of 20 trials of video footage from five children.
The method uses a combination of head tracking, head stabilization, and pupil center and limbus edge tracking to detect OKN.
The pupil center and limbus edge tracking uses a Starburst algorithm to detect limbus edge features.
The method uses a Gabor filter to locate the pupil centroid.
The OKN detection results are based on the analysis of eye velocity signals obtained from three different methods: stabilization, direct subtraction, and Visage SDK.
The method uses a recently proposed OKN detection approach that involves quick phase fitting heuristic criteria.
The study used a commercially available head and eye tracking product (Visage SDK, Visage Technologies) for validation purposes.
The method was tested on video footage from five children with normal vision (ages 21-25 months).
The study involved a clinically trained assessor who annotated a range of frames in which quick phases appeared to be present.
The method uses a simple automatic blink detection based on pupil area measurement.
